offence_severity: imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than two years and which may extend to ten years and also with fine which shall not be less than five thousand rupees
number_of_offences: Number of offences/counts charged: 11; Number of offences finally upheld: 11
premeditation_planning: Yes, the court found premeditation/planning as the accused hatched the criminal conspiracy for pecuniary benefit
motive: pecuniary benefit due to property dispute
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence that the appellant was a member of a 'Gang' and had indulged in anti-social activities, including the conspiracy to commit murder for pecuniary gain.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that the incident was witnessed by passers-by and that the complainant provided a detailed account of the events leading to the murder.
trial_duration: Offence: 23.5.2016; Trial judgment: 27.09.2019; High Court: 10.11.2020; Supreme Court: 26.04.2022
legal_representation: Divyesh Pratap Singh, Sanjay Singh, Vikram Pratap Singh, Ms. Shivangi Singh, Ms. Ishita Bedi, Advs. for the Appellant; Sanjay Kumar Tyagi, Ajay Kumar Prajapati, Prabhat Kumar Rai, Shuvodeep Roy, Shreyas Balaji, Ishaan Borthakur, Advs. for the Respondents
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Dismissed; High Court: Dismissed; Supreme Court: Dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant, Shraddha Gupta, was a member of a 'Gang' and had indulged in anti-social activities mentioned in Section 2(b) of the Gangsters Act, 1986, and therefore could be prosecuted under the Act. They emphasized that the Gangsters Act does not require multiple offences or FIRs for prosecution and that the appellant was part of a conspiracy to commit murder for pecuniary gain.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant was not named in the FIR and was falsely implicated in the case. They contended that solely on the basis of a single FIR/charge sheet, she cannot be charged under the Gangsters Act and that she was not a gang leader or member engaged in anti-social activities.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the definitions of 'Gang' and 'Gangster' under the Gangsters Act, 1986, and held that even a single crime committed by a 'Gang' is sufficient to invoke the Act against its members, provided the activity meets the criteria of anti-social conduct.
precedent_relied_upon: Piyush Kantilal Mehta v. Commissioner of Police, Ahmedabad City 1989 Supp (1) SCC 322; Karansinh Chetansinh Vaghela v. State of Gujarat 2021 SCC onLine Gujarat 1260
